A while ago, I spoke with someone who explicitly told me that Ansar Allah (Houthis) were pursuing regime change in Saudi Arabia. This guy is someone I trust, and he’s not the type to follow the hype or make things up.
Not gonna lie, when he first told me, I thought he was joking or high on khat. I held off on sharing the information because it sounded completely bonkers.
Just days later, a public figure from Ansar Allah (I forgot who) said the same thing. Now, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a spokesman and member of Ansar Allah’s Political Bureau, has repeated it almost word for word.
He said Yemen supports any move or action inside Saudi Arabia aimed at overthrowing Mohammed bin Salman’s rule, and that this support extends to actions by the public, the opposition, or even members of the royal family.
Then, yesterday, The Wall Street Journal published a report saying that Mohammed bin Salman has been moving cautiously between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers, accompanied by handpicked security guards, amid fears of a potential assassination attempt.
Well, it turns out the guy was right about what Ansar Allah is calling for. Regime change in Saudi Arabia still sounds pretty far-fetched, but apparently, this is something they’re openly talking about.

On October 12, North Korea’s General Missile Bureau conducted a test launch of a Hwasong-11C (Hwasong-11Da) tactical ballistic missile, designated KN-30 by the United States, to verify an upgrade to a key component.
The General Missile Bureau described the test as a major success, stating that the upgrade would significantly improve the power and accuracy of all offensive weapons systems.

A grand opening ceremony for the Defense Revolution Museum of the Second Economic Committee was held in Pyongyang, North Korea, on October 11, marking the 81st anniversary of the founding of the Workers’ Party of Korea (WPK).
Official images show the sheer scale of the museum, which houses an extensive collection of military equipment, including multi-axle mobile launchers for intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs).
The museum also appears to have space for virtually everything North Korea has showcased at test sites and military parades over the past 15 years.

Hezbollah has made significant changes to its military structure, dismissing personnel it no longer considers necessary and working to improve its FPV drone capabilities. These efforts range from personnel training to upgrades to the drones themselves, including increased explosive payloads and extended fiber-optic link ranges, now reaching around 30 km, as the group prepares for a potential new war.
The new leadership has opted for a different direction and adopted a new strategy, moving away from tactics that had become obsolete and ineffective against the Israeli army and seeking to adapt to the evolution of warfare in recent years.
